newsitem.title: SWEDEN: Policy can't affect unemployment - Swedish Riksbank.
newsitem.headline: Policy can't affect unemployment - Swedish Riksbank.

text.p: Sweden's Riksbank governor Urban Backstrom on Thursday repeated that monetary policy could not eliminate the effects of poor wage formation and the structural unemployment deriving from it.

"The task of eliminating effects of inefficient wage formation and the ensuing structural unemployment lies outside the scope of monetary policy," Backstrom told the Swedish Employers' Confederation's annual general meeting.
"But it is very much a matter that can be influenced by the labour market parties -- representatives of employers as well as employees," he said.
"A problem lies in the circumstance that the parties do not have to carry the full costs when wage formation functions poorly."

Backstrom called the 1995 wage settlements a failure as they meant wage increases that pushed labour costs higher, necessitating further rationalisation and hampering new recruitment. He called for new views.

"There is certainly a good deal of new thinking about wage formation but the intended norm seems to be to negotiate wage increases at the level for Western Europe, and we are not even there yet," he said.
"Has it not occurred to anyone that this can also lead to unemployment becoming permanently fixed at the level for Western Europe?"
In April Swedish unemployment stood at 8.3 percent, down from 8.4 percent in March but up from 7.5 percent in April last year, according to Statistics Sweden.

Sweden is experiencing jobless growth and much indicates that the structural unemployment has risen, Backstrom said, adding that a poorly functioning labour market could have a negative impact on the financial market.

"A labour market that functions poorly can influence the expectations of savers and investors about the low inflation regime's sustainability and thereby the stability of bond rates and the exchange rate," he said.
He called for cooperation between employers and employees.
"One of the few countries in Europe where employment has risen and unemployment fallen in the past decade is the Netherlands," Backstrom said.
"An important ingredient of the succesful labour market trend there has been the evolution of a consensus."
